title: Constraint-Traceable Liquid-Nitrogen Dewar Design for Low-Noise HTS-SQUID Magnetometry
authors: Xinmin Shi, Bingke Xiang, Lingtong Hou, Wanjuan Tang, Geming Zhang, Shiqun Liu, Ruonan Wang, Yibo Wang, Zhiqiang Cao, Xueshen Wang, Xueying Zhang, Xiaoyang Lin
abstract: Compact high-temperature superconducting quantum interference device (HTS-SQUID) magnetometers require a liquid-nitrogen Dewar that balances operating duration against instrument-envelope and mass constraints. Here we introduced a constraint-traceable design workflow in which body radius and neck-length fraction were scanned under fixed outer-envelope volume and geometry-based mass limits. The longest-duration feasible grid point lay adjacent to the 3.85 kg and 550 mm constraint intersection, predicting 224 h hold time from a body-only initial fill to a residual liquid depth of 10 mm. A reference Dewar was experimentally monitored for 137.3 h, consuming 1.22 L liquid-nitrogen of its initial inventory. A thermal model calibrated over the first 40 h reproduced the remaining 97.3 h. Device measurements at liquid-nitrogen temperature showed a superconducting transition and Fraunhofer-like junction response, a maximum voltage-modulation depth of 36.2 $μ$V, and a median noise level of 41.5 fT Hz$^{-1/2}$ from 100 to 1000 Hz. These results establish a reproducible method for selecting Dewar geometry under coupled constraints and demonstrate compatibility with long-endurance and low-noise HTS-SQUID magnetometer systems.
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive engineering solution for designing a compact Dewar for HTS-SQUID magnetometers, balancing cryogenic endurance against physical size and mass limits. By developing a constraint-traceable thermal model, the authors predict long operational times while simultaneously demonstrating that the system maintains high magnetic sensitivity. This work establishes a robust framework for deploying sensitive quantum sensors in field-deployable, long-duration setups.
main_problem: The paper addresses the engineering challenge of designing a compact liquid-nitrogen Dewar for HTS-SQUID magnetometry that maximizes operational endurance while adhering to strict physical constraints like mass and envelope size.
main_result: The authors established a reproducible, constraint-traceable design workflow that predicts a long hold time (up to 224 h) and successfully demonstrated the compatibility of the cryogenic system with achieving low-noise SQUID measurements (41.5 fT Hz^-1/2).
method: The methodology combines thermal modeling (calculating heat loads from conduction and radiation) with geometric optimization to determine the longest feasible operating time under coupled mass and size constraints.
model_or_system: The physical system is a liquid-nitrogen Dewar containing an HTS-SQUID magnetometer. The model uses heat transfer equations to calculate the rate of liquid nitrogen mass loss, which is then integrated over time to predict the hold duration.
key_observables: Hold time (hours), maximum voltage-modulation depth (36.2 $\mu$V), and median noise level (41.5 fT Hz$^{-1/2}$ from 100 to 1000 Hz).
important_parameters: Maximum model mass ($\le 3.85 	ext{ kg}$) and maximum length ($\le 550 	ext{ mm}$); liquid nitrogen heat capacity ($L_v$).
main_assumptions: The model simplifies complex heat leak sources (like vapor cooling or joints) into effective parameters, and the G10 architecture is assumed to minimize system-level penalties.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the constrained design space for the Dewar geometry, validate the predicted liquid nitrogen mass depletion against experimental measurements, and characterize the SQUID's voltage-flux response and noise spectrum.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the coupled design problem, develops the thermal model and constraint-tracing workflow, validates the model against experimental mass loss data, and finally presents the SQUID characterization results to confirm system performance.
why_interesting: While focused on cryogenics and instrumentation, the rigorous application of coupled constraint optimization and thermal modeling to ensure long-term, stable operation is relevant to any quantum system requiring sustained, controlled environmental conditions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Thermal model and constrained hold-time design space of the liquid-nitrogen Dewar. a, Schematic of the G10 Dewar and the modeled conductive (Qcond) and radiative (Qrad) heat-load paths. b, Calculated liquid-nitrogen hold time, from a body-only initial fill to a residual liquid depth of 10 mm in the body, as a function of body inner radius R and neck-length fraction r = Lneck/L. White contours indicate hold time; the black and blue dashed lines denote the Mmodel = 3.85 kg and L = 550 mm constraints, respectively. The unfrosted region satisfies both constraints. Mmodel is a geometry-based mass proxy.

Figure 2: Hold-time validation and evolution of heat loads in the liquid-nitrogen Dewar. a, Measured remaining liquid-nitrogen mass (open grey circles) and thermal-model prediction (blue line). The vertical dotted line marks the end of the measurement, while the horizontal dashed line indicates the defined endpoint of a 10 mm liquid level in the Dewar body, predicted at approximately 224 h. b, Model-calculated total heat load (Qtotal) and its radiative (Qrad) and conductive (Qcond) components, all of which decrease as the liquid level falls. The approximately 224 h endpoint is a model extrapolation beyond the measured interval.

Figure 3: Superconducting transition and magnetic-field response of a Josephson junction. a, Resistance-temperature curve with an Ambegaokar-Halperin fit to the low-resistance foot. b, Differential-resistance map as functions of magnetic field and bias current. The displayed field is an offset-corrected nominal coordinate.

Figure 4: SQUID modulation and noise performance. a, Voltage-flux curves measured at bias currents from 40 to 70 µA, showing a maximum measured modulation depth of 36.2 µV. The flux coordinate is normalized to the measured response period. b, Noise spectrum measured at 77 K. The gray dashed line indicates the median noise level from 100 to 1000 Hz: 41.5 fT Hz−1/2.
